summary: Describes practices and plans emerging among Internet service providers for deploying IPv6, drawn from a survey of ISPs in early 2010. It identifies technology gaps but makes no recommendations. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 9386.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet providers shared how they planned to roll out IPv6. This collects what they said and points out where tools were missing. A later document replaced it.

questions: what did isps choose for ipv6
subtitle: A 2010 survey of how Internet service providers planned and deployed IPv6

tldr.problem: IPv4 address space exhaustion forces ISPs to choose between squeezing IPv4 harder, stacking NAT layers, or deploying IPv6. Real-world deployment requires understanding ISP needs and technology gaps.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents practices from 31 ISPs surveyed in early 2010, describing their deployment choices, technology preferences, customer readiness timelines, and missing capabilities.
tldr.outcome: Most ISPs preferred dual-stack routing backbones for simplicity. Key gaps remained in CPE support, billing systems, and IPv6-to-IPv4 translation products. This document was replaced by RFC 9386.

today: RFC 6036 is Informational and was replaced by RFC 9386, which provides an updated survey reflecting deployment experience and evolved industry practices.

sections.title: The IPv4 Exhaustion Challenge
sections.content: As IPv4 address space neared exhaustion around 2010, Internet Service Providers faced three paths forward: allocate smaller and smaller IPv4 blocks to customers, deploy layers of Network Address Translation (NAT) to share addresses, or move to IPv6. This RFC captures the preferences and deployment plans of ISPs responding to a 2010 survey, focusing on the third path. The document describes practices already adopted or planned for deployment, not recommendations, recognizing that each ISP's choices depend on its circumstances. It covers addressing, routing, DNS, management, and IPv4-IPv6 coexistence mechanisms, assuming the reader understands IPv6 basics.
sections.plainLanguage: Old Internet addresses are running out. Companies had to pick: squeeze more people onto old addresses, use translation tricks, or switch to new addresses. This RFC shows what the biggest Internet providers actually decided to do.

sections.title: ISP Deployment Practices and Preferences
sections.content: Among 31 responding ISPs (65% European, ranging from 30 to 40 million customers), the overwhelming consensus was to deploy a dual-stack routing backbone where both IPv4 and IPv6 run natively. 94% chose this approach, citing simplicity and cost as the main reasons. Some ISPs deployed 6to4 relays (39%) or Teredo servers (16%) as transition aids. Only three ISPs planned MPLS-based approaches like 6PE. Most ISPs did not plan dedicated IPv6 equipment or network topology restructuring; 77% saw no need to redesign their infrastructure. For address allocation, most offered /48 or /56 prefixes to customers, with some offering multiple prefix sizes. DHCPv6, stateless autoconfiguration, and manual delegation all saw use. By 2010, 42% of ISPs already offered IPv6 as a regular service, though customer adoption remained below 1%. Another 48% had deployment in progress or planned, with most targeting 2010-2013 for regular service launch.
sections.plainLanguage: Most providers just ran IPv4 and IPv6 side by side on the same backbone. It was simple, and they could keep doing things the way they always did. Few wanted to rebuild their whole network for IPv6.

sections.title: Technology Gaps and Missing Products
sections.content: Despite mature fundamentals, significant gaps hampered deployment. Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) was the most commonly mentioned limitation; many ISP-supplied routers and modems could not support IPv6. Mobile handsets, DSLAMs, firewalls, load balancers, traffic management boxes, and billing systems also lagged. Field upgrades were mostly infeasible: only 5 ISPs said devices could be upgraded, 4 said partially, and 10 said no. ISPs requested scalable NAT64/DNS64 products to bridge IPv6-only and IPv4-only traffic, robust dual-stack firewalls that use unified rules instead of separate IPv4 and IPv6 configurations, and IPv6 support in open-source tools. Confusion about PPPoE, RADIUS, prefix delegation, and tunnel brokers indicated documentation gaps. Billing and accounting software readiness was particularly low at 23%. A direct quote from one ISP summarized the challenge: 'Just do it, bit by bit...eating the elephant one mouthful at a time.'
sections.plainLanguage: Home routers didn't understand IPv6. Billing systems couldn't track it. Tools for connecting old and new systems were hard to find. It was manageable one step at a time, but vendors hadn't made everything ready yet.

sections.title: Interworking and Transition Methods
sections.content: ISPs anticipated customers needing to reach both IPv6 and IPv4 services for many years, with the most common estimate being more than ten years of continued IPv4-only application support. Mobile operators were certain they would have IPv6-only customers; fixed ISPs were more skeptical (58% did not expect IPv6-only customers). Only three ISPs considered IP-layer interworking unnecessary. However, only three different ISPs actually deployed or planned NAT-PT translation. About 30% planned some form of NAT64/DNS64, but the products were immature. Some ISPs who had not yet chosen a translator relied on dual-stack clients and hoped customers would configure applications to prefer the appropriate transport. Deployment experience with 6to4 and Teredo varied; some found 6to4 convenient for cable users, others favored 6RD. One very large MPLS operator chose 6PE to avoid an IPv6 IGP, and another planned 6VPE with NAT64 support. Mobile IPv6 (or Nemo) drew little interest: only 19% of ISPs said yes.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers would need both old and new connections for a long time. ISPs weren't sure how to make them work together smoothly, and the tools to translate between them weren't quite ready.

sections.title: Customer Demand and Timeline Trends
sections.content: By early 2010, 61% of ISPs reported that some large customers were requesting IPv6. Predictions for when 10% of all customers would require IPv6 ranged from 2010 to 2017, with 50% adoption expected between 2011 and 2020. Most ISPs needed IPv6 to be a standard service by 2010-2015, with 2011 the most common target. Current customer IPv6 usage was negligible, under 1% for most providers, but ISPs predicted 50% of total traffic would be IPv6 by 2015. Regional differences were modest; large operators occasionally chose more complex solutions like 6PE and DS-lite, while medium and small operators preferred simple dual-stack. A consistent theme emerged: evangelization was essential because many ISP and IT managers were unaware of the urgency, skeptical of IPv4 depletion claims, and unaware of NAT support costs. Operators lacked confidence without real customer experience to guide them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some big customers wanted IPv6, and ISPs guessed it would be a must-have by 2011 or so. But most people still didn't use it, so getting business buy-in was hard, and providers didn't yet know how their customers would actually use it.
